title: SuperHype: Hypergraph Generation via Graph-Superposition Decomposition
one_liner: Generate realistic hypergraphs by breaking them into layers that stack on top of each other, then rebuilding them layer by layer.
lead: Real networks often have connections between groups of things at once, not just pairs. Drug compounds form cliques where multiple atoms bond together; patient groups share multiple diseases and medicines. But these multi-way connections (called hypergraphs) are so hard to represent that most software just ignores them or loses information. SuperHype treats each hyperedge (a connection among three or more things) as layers stacked on top of each other, turning the whole thing into a regular multi-layer graph that a machine can learn from.

problem.h2: Hypergraphs are hard to write down and generate
paras: Most real networks are not just pairs of things talking to each other. In healthcare, a treatment can connect many patients at once (a disease outbreak, a shared medication). In chemistry, atoms in a molecule form groups where five atoms bond together in one spot. These multi-way connections are called hyperedges, and a network made of them is a hypergraph.

The problem: no one has a simple way to write down a hypergraph on a computer without either (a) throwing away important details, or (b) using math so complicated that learning from it takes forever. Earlier methods try to write each hyperedge as multiple ordinary edges (pairwise connections), but that splits one real thing into many fake pieces. Other methods hide the hyperedges inside high-dimensional lists so abstract that a learning model can barely extract the true structure.

callout.html: You cannot apply standard graph learning tools to hypergraphs because hypergraphs break the rules those tools were built on.

panels.title: 1. The real thing

panels.caption: One connection, many atoms, one moment.

panels.title: 2. Naive way breaks it
panels.caption: Splitting one hyperedge into three separate pairwise edges loses the group.

panels.title: 3. Superposition: layer it
panels.caption: Encode the hyperedge as stacked layers, each layer a regular edge.

panels.title: 4. Neural network sees all layers

panels.title: 5. Full hypergraph rebuilt
panels.caption: Output: new hypergraph with real multi-way connections intact.

steps.text: Take each hyperedge and write it as a separate layer in a stack.
Mark which nodes appear in which layers and track triplet patterns.
Random noise starts at the top layer, gradually resolves into real connections.
Each layer looks at others' patterns to keep multi-way groups intact.
Stitch layers back together to form a complete, valid hypergraph.

paras: Instead of trying to learn a hypergraph all at once as one blob, SuperHype breaks it into a stack of layers (one per hyperedge) and learns each layer as a regular pairwise graph. Then it glues them back together. The object it moves is the representation — from an abstract multi-way blob to a concrete stack of simple graphs.

hidden.h2: Layer alignment: are all layers saying the same thing?
hidden.name: Layer agreement strength
paras: When you split a hyperedge across layers, you create a problem: each layer only sees pairwise connections between two nodes at a time. If the layers work independently, they contradict each other — one layer says A-B are connected, another says B-C are connected, but no layer 'remembers' that A, B, and C all bonded together in one instant. Layer agreement strength is the degree to which all layers align on the same nodes and edges.

SuperHype measures this by having each layer look at other layers' patterns so that connections from one layer reinforce the original multi-way structure in others. The auxiliary features explicitly mark which nodes co-occur across layers, and triplet pooling (summarizing patterns of three-node groups) checks consistency.

heat.caption: Darker: stronger agreement that this layer preserves the original hyperedge structure.

reads.html: Layers that agree on which nodes matter are layers that respect the original multi-way group.
Cross-layer pattern-matching and triplet pooling enforce consistency so the diffusion does not fragment the hyperedge.

mechanism.h2: Why layering and cross-layer pattern-matching keep the structure intact
paras: Here is the core idea: a hyperedge is a single event where multiple atoms or agents act together. If you just split it into pairwise edges and train them separately, each one learns independently, and there is no reason they should 'remember' they were part of the same group. The model can generate A-B and B-C and C-D edges that never co-occur, breaking the original hyperedge.

SuperHype fixes this by (1) putting all pairwise edges from one hyperedge into one layer so they stay close in the network, and (2) having each layer look at others so when the model is generating layer 1, it can see which nodes appear in layer 2 and layer 3 as well. If node B appears in multiple layers, this cross-layer pattern-matching learns to strengthen B's connections in all layers to reflect the multi-way constraint. Auxiliary features like 'node degree across layers' make this even clearer — if node B has degree 3 across all layers (appears in 3 hyperedges), the model can enforce that pattern.

Finally, triplet pooling (a way of summarizing patterns of three connected nodes) directly measures whether the paper's move worked: are there many triples of nodes that stay together across layers? If yes, the hyperedge structure is preserved. If no, the layers have drifted apart.

stages.s: Split into layers (one per edge-pair within the group)
Add node co-occurrence and triplet features
Stitch layers back into a full hypergraph

math.words: Reconstruction loss for each layer plus a penalty if triplet patterns in layer i differ from triplet patterns in layer j
math.equation: L_total = sum_layers L_recon(layer_i) + lambda * sum_{i,j} distance(triplets_i, triplets_j)
symbols: how wrong the generated layer i is compared to real data
counts of three-node groups in layer i
how different layer i and layer j are
how much to penalize disagreement between layers

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Real data: hyperedge (A, B, C, D) becomes 4 layers: [A-B, B-C, C-D, D-A].
If model generates layer 1 with triplet (A,B,C): count 0, count mismatch = 1.
Model learns: include triplet (A,B,C) in layer 1 to avoid penalty and reduce layer disagreement.

math.note: Cross-layer pattern-matching amplifies this signal: if node B is present and active in layers 1, 2, and 3, the model's cross-checking learns to pass that information back so all layers keep B's connections strong.

items.html: If cross-layer pattern-matching is weak or the auxiliary features are incomplete, layers can learn different node sets, fragmenting the hyperedge.
Computing all three-node groups in every layer costs time, so this method is slower on huge graphs than pairwise approximations.

items.b: Large hyperedges (20+ nodes) blow up layers.
items.html: A hyperedge with 20 nodes creates 190 pairwise layer connections; the model has to learn and store all of them.
With strong cross-layer pattern-matching and node-co-occurrence features, the layers stay coherent and the hyperedge structure is reproduced faithfully.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small synthetic hypergraph (e.g., a clique of 4 nodes, a clique of 5 nodes, a clique of 3 nodes — 3 hyperedges total). Train SuperHype on this. Generate 10 new hypergraphs. For each generated hypergraph, measure (1) whether the cliques are preserved (do all pairs within each clique appear?), and (2) whether new edges stay inside the original groups (no spurious cross-clique edges). Count how many of 10 generated hyperedges exactly match the original clique structure.
demo.metric_eq: Hyperedge recovery = (number of generated hyperedges matching original groups) / (total generated hyperedges)
demo.closing: The demo must show that SuperHype recovers the original clique structure in at least 80 percent of generated hyperedges, proving that layering and cross-checking preserve the multi-way grouping.
